name: Erik Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The café owners at Cedar Bookkeeping drop their till reports on my desk in all sorts of shapes, so I start by putting the dates in order. I'm 43, a junior accountant with a bachelor's degree in accounting, and I still need the senior to catch tax details I miss. Getting the week's cash to match the bank is satisfying; having to phone an owner at closing time for one missing page isn't.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and how do pay, savings and new software fit?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Noor works at a bakery counter, and our two children, ten and thirteen, know exactly when the mortgage payment is due because we all watch spending that week. I earn typical pay for this accounting job, we have about three months of expenses saved, and there are some firms nearby. I use AI now and then for a draft after another accountant has tried it, but I check every till figure. I believe people should earn and learn on the job, with family helping first when a bill gets hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a faster way to sort till slips is fine if I can still trace every line to a receipt. I don't want a café owner handed a number neither of us understands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior job stays, though I still make mistakes and need the senior's check. Three months saved helps, but the mortgage and school uniforms mean even a short fall in hours would matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep matching the till slips to bank deposits and use an AI draft only after the senior has tested it. In the first year I'd add seventy a month to our mortgage buffer by repairing my old bicycle rather than replacing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about money even with little AI change. The family is steady, but my junior chair is not guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of mistake still gets past you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A card refund can sit a day later than the sale, and I sometimes put both in the same week. The senior asks me to follow the bank date back to the till slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would the bicycle saving last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: As long as the frame is safe, probably another year. Seventy a month isn't a fortune, but the mortgage account grows without touching the children's shoes.

I would keep a **senior check** on café returns.
think: My **junior job** probably holds, although I still miss some tax details.
A short **hours cut** would still matter beside mortgage and school costs.
do: Keep matching **till slips** to bank deposits with senior review.
Save **seventy monthly** by repairing my bicycle instead of replacing it.
feel: He feels **uneasy** because a short hours cut would strain family bills.

fieldNote: His three-month cushion softens, but does not erase, **mortgage pressure** in a plateau.

steps.text: Keep matching cafe till slips to bank deposits with senior review

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners to show us which parts of a café return the system handles and who checks the result. A paid lesson would help more than another email telling us to keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my day is sorting, checking and writing to owners, so the software reaches my desk quickly. I'm a junior who still needs help; the firm might cut a day from my rota before it cuts anyone senior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a paid half-day beside the senior to test the tool on ten closed café files, and keep a list of wrong totals. In the first year of steady change, if my paid days fall below four a week, I'd apply only for posted junior accounting roles at the two firms across the river while keeping any hours here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing a day of pay. Noor's bakery wage would not fill the mortgage gap on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm won't pay for that half-day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the current returns with the senior's checks and wait for a funded place. I can read the tool's instructions at home, but I would not put live client data into it by myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would school pickup work if you found another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the new start time before accepting a written offer, because I collect our younger child on Tuesdays. Noor could cover only if her bakery shift actually ends in time.

do: Test **ten closed café files** beside the senior on paid time if offered.

Apply for **posted across-river junior roles** below four paid days, keeping current hours until a written offer meets pickup timing.
feel: He feels **anxious** because a lost day could strain the mortgage.

fieldNote: He is willing to test after a **paid supervised slot**, but will keep current work if refused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our café clients that full AGI in 2028 could prepare the accounts, so we should be honest about what a person still checks. I would ask the partners to give the junior staff a dated answer about hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The 2028 date reaches my desk work; robots around 2031 don't give me three extra years. I expect my junior days to be cut, perhaps the whole post, and Noor's counter work could also face robots later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now we'd cancel the holiday deposit and add that eighty a month to our mortgage buffer. In the first year after 2028, if my post ends, I'd apply for advertised paid accounts-control roles nearby and take a confirmed weekend shift at the market bakery only if Noor can handle the children at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because the mortgage needs two wages and I expect one to shrink. Three months of savings is time to search, not a cure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a course in another trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not with the mortgage reserve. I'd take a paid apprenticeship only after an employer writes down the wage, start date and hours; until then I'd keep any paid accounts shifts I can get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no bakery shift is available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my brother to cover one school pickup while I interview, but I would not budget an unoffered shift as income. We would cut restaurant meals first and keep the reserve for the loan.

I would ask for a **dated junior-hours answer** before 2028.
think: My **junior days** may be cut when AGI reaches desk work in 2028.
Noor’s **counter work** could face robots around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to find out whether a paid bookkeeper role remains when the simple returns get cheap. The firm should let us practise the harder work before it takes the juniors off the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031 I would still owe on the mortgage, even if the children are taller than me. AGI can handle my accounts desk then; Noor's counter work may face robots around 2034, so both wages need a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Cedar Bookkeeping for paid practice on café payroll disputes next spring, with the senior watching the first cases. In the first year after 2031, if the firm cuts my days, I'd apply for posted salaried payroll posts at the local college; if no vacancy appears, I'd keep any funded accounting hours and our buffer rather than resign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but five years gives us time to pay down part of the mortgage. I won't call an unpaid course a career move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test whether you can handle payroll?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd reconcile a month's wage slips with the café's bank payments under the senior's eye. The firm must pay for the practice time, because a mistake would be mine to fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for the college job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a written salary offer that covers the mortgage and a start time that lets one of us collect our younger child. I wouldn't move the family for an interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets our family pay down the loan and lets the firm show what work a person still does. I would ask for a real paid path, not an evening course we fund ourselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036 I would still need a wage if the mortgage is not cleared. But ten years of two incomes could shrink the loan enough that I can take a different salaried role; robots around 2039 may change Noor's counter shifts later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add a hundred monthly to mortgage principal while we both have full hours and take a paid bookkeeping qualification only if a local employer posts a job requiring it and covers study time. In the first year after 2036, if my return hours end, I'd apply for that posted salaried role; if no funded path exists, I'd keep available paid firm work and use our buffer only for bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, but there is time to lower the loan before the desk changes. I cannot count on a job that has not been posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not save the hundred instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three-month reserve already gives us a short search window, and reducing principal lowers what we owe every month. If one of us loses hours before then, I would stop extra payments and hold the cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the children when they leave school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn a trade they can explain to another person, even if the tools change. We can help with fees only after the mortgage is current.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my junior days could vanish before the mortgage is much smaller. Paid supervised practice and an advertised job with a stated wage and start date would help. A course is only useful if a real employer will pay for the work afterward.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who looks after the children while a parent retrains after work. A plan with no childcare slot is a plan our family cannot use.

headlineQuote: A plan with no childcare slot is a plan our family cannot use.
portrait: Erik, **43**, is a junior café-accounts worker at Cedar Bookkeeping with an accounting bachelor’s degree.
He earns **typical pay**, has three months saved, a mortgage, two school-age children and some nearby accounting firms.
He uses AI **occasionally after colleagues** test it and still needs senior help with tax details.
He worries about **junior-hour cuts** in 2028 and ties retraining or job moves to pay, vacancy and childcare.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his junior days before the mortgage shrinks enough.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid supervised practice** and an advertised job with wage and start date would help.
